title: Wilson Disease
subject: Pathology
summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal‑recessive disorder of copper metabolism causing hepatic, neurologic and psychiatric disease. Diagnosis relies on low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper and Kayser‑Fleischer rings, with staging guiding treatment.

sections.p: A genetic defect in ATP7B impairs biliary copper excretion, leading to copper accumulation in liver, brain and other organs.
b: Autosomal‑recessive ATP7B mutation
Low serum ceruloplasmin (<0.2 g/L)
Kayser‑Fleischer rings on slit‑lamp exam

sections.p: Staging uses hepatic and neurologic criteria; the Leipzig score (≥4 points) confirms diagnosis.
b: Leipzig score ≥4 = definite Wilson disease
Mild: isolated hepatic elevation, no neuro signs
Moderate: hepatic decompensation or early neuro signs
Severe: fulminant liver failure, advanced neuro disability

sections.p: The primary cause is inherited ATP7B mutation; secondary copper overload from chronic liver disease or excess supplementation can mimic it.
b: Inherited ATP7B loss‑of‑function (most common worldwide)
Rare: copper‑containing herbal remedies
Differential: chronic hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, malaria‑related hemolysis

sections.p: Patients may present with hepatic, neurologic or psychiatric features, often in late adolescence or early adulthood.
b: Hepatic: jaundice, hepatomegaly, ascites, abnormal LFTs
Neurologic: tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, gait disturbance
Psychiatric: personality change, depression, psychosis
Kayser‑Fleischer rings in >90% with neuro disease

t.b: Is copper transport protein low? → <0.2 g/L supports Wilson disease
Is copper excretion high? → >100 µg/24 h confirms excess copper
Are Kayser‑Fleischer rings present? → Positive rings indicate copper deposition in cornea
Is there hepatic injury? → Elevated enzymes suggest liver involvement
Is there liver fibrosis or cirrhosis? → May show coarse echotexture; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs of chronic liver disease
Are basal ganglia changes present? → Hyperintensity in putamen supports neurologic disease

sections.p: Untreated copper overload leads to irreversible organ damage.
b: Acute liver failure (coagulopathy, encephalopathy)
Severe neuro decline (parkinsonism, dysphagia)
Hemolytic anemia during decompensation
Renal tubular dysfunction

sections.p: Remove excess copper, prevent re‑accumulation and treat organ dysfunction.
b: Chelation: D‑penicillamine or trientine – bind copper for urinary excretion
Zinc salts – block intestinal copper absorption
Avoid vitamin C high doses (increases copper absorption)
Liver transplant for fulminant hepatic failure or decompensated cirrhosis
Supportive care: diuretics for ascites, neuro‑rehab for movement disorders

sections.p: Lifelong monitoring is required; family screening is essential.
b: Quarterly urinary copper while on chelators
Annual liver ultrasound or elastography
Neurologic exam each visit
Screen siblings with ceruloplasmin and genetic testing

sections.p: Conditions that cause similar hepatic or neurologic signs.
b: Hemochromatosis – iron overload, high ferritin, not low ceruloplasmin
Autoimmune hepatitis – high IgG, ANA positive
Alcoholic liver disease – history of alcohol, AST:ALT >2
Neurodegenerative disorders (Parkinson’s, Huntington’s) – no copper signs

sections.p: Certain tests may be normal early in disease.
b: Ceruloplasmin can be normal in acute liver failure; rely on urinary copper
Kayser‑Fleischer rings absent in isolated hepatic disease; do not exclude diagnosis
MRI may be normal in early neurologic involvement

whenToSeekHelp: New onset severe neuro decline (speech, swallowing)

faq.q: Why is zinc used in Wilson disease?
faq.a: Zinc induces metallothionein in enterocytes, which binds copper and prevents its absorption.

faq.q: Can Wilson disease present without eye findings?
faq.a: Yes, isolated hepatic disease may lack Kayser‑Fleischer rings; diagnosis relies on labs and genetic testing.
Transplant removes the diseased organ and restores copper excretion, effectively curing hepatic disease, but neurologic damage may persist.

exam: A 16‑year‑old presents with tremor and mild jaundice – what is the next diagnostic step? — Perform slit‑lamp exam for Kayser‑Fleischer rings and order 24‑hour urinary copper.
How does the Leipzig score differentiate Wilson disease from other liver disorders? — Points from ceruloplasmin, urinary copper, rings, genetic test; ≥4 confirms diagnosis.
Why is D‑penicillamine preferred over high‑dose vitamin C in acute decompensation? — Penicillamine chelates copper for excretion; vitamin C increases copper absorption and worsens overload.
A patient on zinc therapy develops anemia – what should you check? — Ensure zinc dose is not excessive and assess for copper deficiency; adjust therapy accordingly.
What are the indications for liver transplantation in Wilson disease? — Acute liver failure, decompensated cirrhosis, or refractory hepatic copper overload despite chelation.

How would you differentiate Wilson disease from hemochromatosis on laboratory testing? — Wilson disease shows low ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper; hemochromatosis shows high ferritin and transferrin saturation.

In a low‑resource setting without MRI, how can you assess neurologic involvement? — Detailed neurologic exam focusing on movement disorders, speech, and ocular signs; use bedside fundoscopy for rings.

What emergency management is required for a patient with Wilson disease presenting in fulminant hepatic failure? — Admit to ICU, correct coagulopathy, start chelation, arrange urgent transplant evaluation.
